newsitem.title: USA: U.S. regulator backs new credit union rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. regulator backs new credit union rules.

text.p: Federal regulators took steps Thursday to limit the fallout from a recent court decision that could force millions of employees out of lower-cost credit unions.

The National Credit Union Administration approved several changes to rules governing membership policy, including a provision that would allow employees of different companies to belong to the same credit union if the companies are in related fields.
The agency acted after a federal judge ruled that federal credit unions could not admit members who did not share a "common bond" of occupation.
But the agency's own definition of a "common bond" was limited to employees who worked for the same company or affiliated companies. The broader definition would cast a wider net.

The action came amid widespread concern in the industry that the court ruling would not only limit the growth of credit unions but could ultimately force some 3,500 credit unions to expel current members who work for other businesses.
"What we are doing today will substantially and significantly alleviate some of the pain," NCUA Chairman Norman D'Amours said. "We don't consider this fixed."

Credit unions are non-profit organisations that generally offer lower rates on loans and higher savings rates than banks. They enjoy tax advantages that banks contend have given them unfair advantages, allowing the favourable terms.

A spokeswoman for the American Bankers Association, which has been waging a legal battle against the credit-union regulators in recent years, said the trade group will probably review the new policy to "see if it squares" with the judge's ruling.
D'Amours said the agency would continue to pursue legal and legislative remedies in the wake of the court decision.

It remains unclear just how the ruling should be interpreted or whether credit unions will be forced to expel current members who work for companies in unrelated fields. Such issues are to be discussed at a meeting with the judge in early December.

Regulators began allowing credit unions to take in members from various groups in the early 1980s if a company or other organisation that employed many of a credit union's members got into financial difficulty.
NCUA attorneys maintain that their new membership rules were consistent with the recent court ruling calling for a common bond of occupation.
The board also authorised a "group community" charter, allowing a credit union to choose to serve specific occupational, association and community groups within a well-defined area.
